name: Angkor / Siem Reap
scope: The temple-city of the Khmer Empire on the plain north of the town of Siem Reap, Cambodia. T1: Angkor Wat is the LARGEST religious monument ever built — a single temple, moat and towers covering ~160 hectares, so vast its five-towered silhouette sits on Cambodia's national flag (invert: the flag/size is the hook, 'largest religious monument' the answer). T2: almost every Khmer temple faces the sunrise, but Angkor Wat's main gate faces WEST — the direction of the setting sun and the dead — hinting it doubled as King Suryavarman II's funerary temple. T3: at nearby Ta Prohm the jungle never left — giant silk-cotton and strangler-fig roots pour over the walls, holding the ruins together and prying them apart at once (the 'Tomb Raider temple'; teach 'strangler fig'). T4: laser scanners flown over the forest (LiDAR) stripped the canopy to reveal Angkor was the LARGEST city of the pre-industrial world — a sprawling grid of roads, canals and neighborhoods that held ~700,000–900,000 people (teach 'LiDAR'). T5: the Khmer engineered a hydraulic megacity — vast rectangular reservoirs called barays (the West Baray is ~8 km long) stored monsoon water to irrigate rice through the dry season, and when the water network failed the city was abandoned (teach 'baray'). Extra rungs: the ~200 giant serene stone faces of the Bayon; the ~50 m bas-relief gallery of the 'Churning of the Sea of Milk'; the five lotus-bud towers built as Mount Meru; the causeway of gods-and-demons at Angkor Thom's south gate; the pink sandstone miniatures of Banteay Srei.
source: Grokipedia (West_Baray); Wikipedia (Angkor Wat, Ta Prohm, Angkor); Evans et al., 'Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar,' PNAS 2013 (PMC3732978); NASA Earth Observatory (Angkor)
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER, scene-led, invert the superlative into the stem and make the knowable thing the answer. Key accuracy rail: Angkor Wat is the largest RELIGIOUS monument (not 'largest building'); the west-facing/funerary reading is scholarly interpretation, phrase as 'suggesting', not settled fact. Dinner-test payoff: the LiDAR rung — a hidden megacity of ~750,000 under the jungle. Frame Angkor as a PLANNED hydraulic megacity engineered by a full civilization, never a 'mysterious lost jungle temple' or 'primitive' ruin. Distractors stay live with other real Khmer/Asian temples (Borobudur, Bagan, Prambanan, Bayon vs Angkor Wat).
history_overlap: The Khmer Empire's political narrative (Suryavarman II's reign, Jayavarman VII, the 15th-c. abandonment as a dynastic story) belongs to the history bank; keep every rung anchored to the PHYSICAL place — the monument, its orientation, the fig-wrapped ruins, the hydraulic city and its barays.

name: Bagan
scope: The medieval temple-plain on a bend of the Irrawaddy (Ayeyarwady) River in central Myanmar. T1: on a dry plain stand over TWO THOUSAND surviving brick temples and pagodas — the ruins of a capital where kings once built more than 10,000 (invert: the count is the hook, 'the plain of Bagan' the answer). T2: at dawn hot-air balloons drift over a sea of red-brick spires; the graceful, perfectly symmetric white Ananda Temple, lit by hidden windows, is called the masterpiece of Bagan. T3: Bagan's temples are built almost entirely of fired BRICK, not stone — which is why a 2016 magnitude-6.8 earthquake could crack and topple hundreds of them (nearly 400 damaged). T4: the city sits in Myanmar's 'dry zone', in the rain shadow of the Arakan mountains, beside the Irrawaddy — the great river artery whose water made a desert-edge capital possible (teach 'rain shadow'). T5: that shaking came from the Sagaing Fault, one of Earth's major strike-slip faults where the India and Sunda plates grind past each other — the same force that both builds Myanmar's landscape and threatens the temples (teach 'strike-slip fault'). Extra rungs: the massive Dhammayangyi, a solid brick pyramid whose inner corridors were mysteriously bricked up; the tall Thatbyinnyu; the gilded bell-shaped Shwezigon, prototype of the Burmese stupa; Shwesandaw, the 'sunset pagoda' you climb for the view over the plain.
source: Wikipedia (Bagan, Ananda Temple, Sagaing Fault); UNESCO World Heritage List (Bagan, inscribed 2019); phys.org and ResearchGate reports on the 2016 M6.8 earthquake damage
framing_note: Voice: scene-led, the temple-sea at dawn is the setting; invert the '2,000 / 10,000' counts into the stem. Key accuracy rail: state 'over 2,000 surviving' vs 'more than 10,000 originally built' precisely — do not conflate. Dinner-test payoff: the brick-built T3 rung tied to the 2016 quake (why they fall). Lane border: the temples are the wonder, not the Pagan Kingdom's dynastic wars. Distractors stay live with other real temple-fields/rivers (Angkor, Ayutthaya, Mekong vs Irrawaddy).

name: Yogyakarta: Borobudur & Prambanan
scope: Two rival 9th-century masterpieces on the volcanic plain near Yogyakarta, central Java. T1: rising from the jungle is the LARGEST Buddhist temple on Earth — not a tower but a stone mountain of nine stacked terraces you climb like a pilgrim, crowned by one great dome (Borobudur). T2: seen from above Borobudur is a giant MANDALA, a Buddhist diagram of the cosmos; pilgrims walk clockwise up past ~2,672 carved relief panels that tell the path from earthly desire to enlightenment (teach 'mandala'). T3: on the top three round terraces sit 72 bell-shaped stone stupas, each a stone lattice cage hiding a seated Buddha inside; the crowning central stupa is deliberately EMPTY — the void of enlightenment. T4: for centuries Borobudur lay buried under volcanic ash and jungle from nearby Mount Merapi, one of the world's most active volcanoes, until it was dug out in the 1800s. T5: a short drive away soar the spires of Prambanan, the largest Hindu temple in Indonesia — its central Shiva tower rises ~47 m, so Java holds two giant rival temples, Buddhist and Hindu, built within a century of each other. Extra rungs: Borobudur assembled from ~2 million interlocking volcanic blocks WITHOUT mortar; the hidden 'buried foot' reliefs at its base; Prambanan's carved Ramayana galleries; both temples fed by the fertile ash of the same volcanic Kewu plain.
source: Wikipedia (Borobudur, Prambanan); Guinness World Records (largest Buddhist temple, 2012); National Geographic (Borobudur Temple Compounds); UNESCO World Heritage (Borobudur, Prambanan)
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; invert 'largest Buddhist temple' into the scene. Key accuracy rail: Borobudur is the largest BUDDHIST temple / monument (Guinness); Prambanan the largest HINDU temple in Indonesia — keep the two claims distinct. Handle the burial honestly: it was buried by volcanic ash/jungle and cleared in the 1800s — do NOT say a colonial figure 'discovered' a temple local villagers had always known; phrase as 'cleared / excavated'. Dinner-test payoff: the 72 stone bells each hiding a Buddha, over one empty central dome. Distractors stay live with Angkor Wat, Bagan, and Prambanan-vs-Borobudur cross-pairs.
history_overlap: The Sailendra / Medang (Mataram) dynastic history belongs to the history/ancient bank; keep rungs on the monuments' form, the mandala structure, the volcanic burial, and Merapi.

name: Bangkok
scope: The Thai capital on the delta of the Chao Phraya River. T1: the city Thais call Krung Thep, 'City of Angels', has a full ceremonial name so long — 168 letters in one word — that it holds the world record for the longest place name on Earth (invert: the record is the hook). T2: inside the Grand Palace glows the Emerald Buddha, Thailand's most sacred image, carved from a single block of green JADE (not emerald), whose golden seasonal robes only the King may change. T3: a few steps away at Wat Pho reclines a gilded Buddha 46 m long and 15 m high, the soles of its feet inlaid with mother-of-pearl showing 108 auspicious signs. T4: Wat Pho is also the birthplace and living school of traditional Thai massage, its healing points carved onto the temple's walls — a cultural creation born in this exact place. T5: Bangkok grew on the flat, flood-prone Chao Phraya delta, once so laced with canals (khlongs) that Westerners called it the 'Venice of the East'; floating markets still sell from boats on the water (teach 'delta'). Extra rungs: Wat Arun, the 'Temple of Dawn', its riverside spire studded with broken porcelain; Rattanakosin, the old royal island ringed by canals; the golden chedi of the Grand Palace.
source: Guinness World Records (longest place name); Wikipedia (Bangkok, Wat Pho, Wat Phra Kaew / Emerald Buddha, Chao Phraya River); emerald-buddha.com (Reclining Buddha dimensions)
framing_note: Voice: scene-led; put the 168-letter record and the physical measurements in the stem, keep the named thing the answer. Key accuracy rail: the Emerald Buddha is JADE, not emerald — that is itself a rung; the reclining Buddha is 46 m long / 15 m high. Dinner-test payoff: the mother-of-pearl feet with 108 signs, or the 168-letter name. Lane border (COOKING): the floating/canal market is a WATERSCAPE the geography bank owns; the dishes it sells belong to the cooking bank — a one-line mention is fine, no food-origin rung. Distractors stay live with other real Thai temples/rivers.

name: Singapore
scope: The equatorial island city-state at the tip of the Malay Peninsula. T1: Singapore is a tiny island that keeps getting BIGGER — it has grown roughly a quarter larger (from ~582 to ~723 km²) by piling sand into the sea, making it the fastest-growing country on Earth by land reclamation (invert: 'a country that keeps growing' is the hook; teach 'land reclamation'). T2: on the waterfront stand the Supertrees of Gardens by the Bay — 18 towering steel 'trees' up to 50 m tall, wrapped in living plants, that harvest rainwater and glow at night. T3: with almost no land to spare, Singapore dammed the sea — the Marina Barrage turned a saltwater bay in the heart of downtown into a giant FRESHWATER reservoir for drinking water. T4: having no big rivers and no room, Singapore imports so much sand to build new land that some neighboring countries banned selling it to them. T5: Singapore sits almost exactly on the equator, guarding the Strait of Malacca — the narrow sea-gate through which a huge share of the world's ships and oil must squeeze — which is why the city became one of Earth's greatest ports (teach 'strait / chokepoint'). Extra rungs: Jewel Changi's Rain Vortex, the world's tallest indoor waterfall; the 'garden city' of vertical greenery and rooftop parks; reclaimed Jurong Island, built by merging small islands into a petrochemical hub.
source: Wikipedia (Land reclamation in Singapore, Gardens by the Bay); Guinness World Records (fastest-growing country through land reclamation); Mothership.SG (25% land-area growth); BiblioAsia NLB ('Land From Sand')
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the paradox of a country GROWING is the hook. Key accuracy rail: quote the reclamation growth as ~24–25% (from ~582 km² in the 1960s to ~723 km²) — do not round to '50%'; the Supertrees number 18, 25–50 m tall. Dinner-test payoff: the land-that-grows-by-importing-sand pairing (T1/T4). Distractors stay live with other real reclaimed/port cities and Asian gardens. This is settled engineering wonder — no stance needed.

name: Shwedagon Pagoda / Yangon
scope: Myanmar's holiest shrine, crowning Singuttara Hill in Yangon. T1: rising nearly 100 m over the city, the Shwedagon Pagoda is a mountain of GOLD — its great bell-shaped stupa sheathed head to foot in real gold plates and gold leaf renewed by the faithful (invert: 'a mountain of gold' is the hook). T2: at its very tip sits a diamond-studded orb crowned by a single ~72-carat diamond that flashes red, then green, then white as you walk around the base. T3: the shrine is said to enshrine relics of four Buddhas, including eight hairs of the Buddha Gautama — which is why pilgrims circle it clockwise, barefoot. T4: around the base sit eight 'planetary posts', one for each day of the Burmese week (which splits Wednesday into two) — worshippers pour water over the corner for the day they were born. Extra rungs: the stupa's terraced octagonal base; the ring of smaller golden shrines and bells; the covered stairways guarded by giant chinthe (lion-dogs) at the four gates.
source: Wikipedia (Shwedagon Pagoda); official shwedagonpagoda.org.mm; renown-travel.com (99.36 m height)
framing_note: Voice: scene-led; the gold and the crowning diamond are the hooks. Key accuracy rail: the relics (eight Buddha hairs) are religious tradition — attribute as 'is said to enshrine', do not assert as physical fact; sources vary on the top diamond (72 vs 76 carat), so phrase 'about 72 carats'. Dinner-test payoff: the color-flashing diamond at the very tip. Respect the sacred site plainly — no smug secular dismissal and no advertising-brochure gush. Distractors stay live with other gold/relic stupas (Shwezigon, Kyaiktiyo Golden Rock).

name: Ayutthaya
scope: The ruined former royal capital of Siam, an hour north of Bangkok. T1: Ayutthaya was built on an ISLAND — a moat-ringed city on land made where three rivers (the Chao Phraya, Lopburi and Pa Sak) meet (invert: the island-at-three-rivers is the hook). T2: at Wat Mahathat a stone Buddha's HEAD rests serenely at ground level, slowly cradled and swallowed by the twisting roots of a strangler fig (teach 'strangler fig'). T3: in its golden age around 1700 Ayutthaya was one of the LARGEST cities in the world — perhaps a million people — a cosmopolitan trading capital where Portuguese, Dutch, Chinese and Japanese merchants each had their own quarter. T4: the city died in a single blow — in 1767 a Burmese army sacked and burned it and stripped the gold from its Buddhas; the Siamese never rebuilt it, founding a new capital downriver that became Bangkok. Extra rungs: the three bullet-shaped prangs of Wat Phra Si Sanphet; the row of headless Buddhas along the brick galleries; the giant reclining Buddha at Wat Lokayasutharam.
source: Wikipedia (Ayutthaya Kingdom, Ayutthaya Historical Park); Britannica (Ayutthaya); UNESCO World Heritage (Historic City of Ayutthaya)
framing_note: Voice: scene-led; the island geography and the fig-root head are the anchors. Key accuracy rail: the tree at Wat Mahathat is commonly a strangler fig/bodhi — say 'tree roots (a strangler fig)', not a specific unverifiable species; founded 1350, sacked 1767. Dinner-test payoff: the serene Buddha head cradled in fig roots (T2). Distractors stay live with other real ruined capitals (Sukhothai, Angkor, Bagan) and Thai rivers.
history_overlap: The 1767 Burmese sack as a war narrative is a history-bank episode; here it is the endpoint that explains the RUINS — keep the rung on the abandoned physical city, not the campaign.

name: Luang Prabang
scope: The old royal town on a river peninsula in northern Laos. T1: Luang Prabang sits on a finger of land where the Mekong meets the Nam Khan — a peninsula between two rivers whose waters flow side by side in visibly different colors (invert: the two-color confluence is the hook). T2: every dawn hundreds of barefoot, saffron-robed monks walk in a long silent line through the streets while kneeling townspeople place sticky rice into their bowls — the alms-giving called Tak Bat. T3: climb the 300-plus steps of Mount Phousi in the town's center to watch the two rivers curve around gilded temple roofs at sunset. T4: south of town, Kuang Si Falls tumbles over pale LIMESTONE terraces into pools of impossible turquoise — the color comes from calcium carbonate dissolved out of the rock and re-deposited as travertine (teach 'limestone / travertine'). Extra rungs: the golden royal temple of Wat Xieng Thong with its sweeping low roofs; the town's status as a whole UNESCO-listed living townscape (1995); the confluence sandbars that appear in the dry season.
source: Wikipedia (Luang Prabang, Kuang Si Falls); UNESCO World Heritage (Town of Luang Prabang, 1995); Rainforest Cruises (Tak Bat guide)
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the two-river peninsula and the dawn procession are the scenes. Key accuracy rail: Kuang Si's turquoise is a real earth-process (dissolved limestone / travertine), not dye — that IS the T4 wonder; the alms ritual is a living practice, describe it respectfully and plainly (no advertising gush). Dinner-test payoff: the turquoise travertine pools, or the silent dawn line of monks. Distractors stay live with other confluences and limestone falls (Plitvice, Pamukkale).

name: Hanoi Old Quarter
scope: The historic core of Vietnam's capital on the Red River delta. T1: in the heart of Hanoi lies the Old Quarter, a maze famous as the '36 Streets', where each lane was once home to a single guild — and many are STILL named for the goods sold there (Silk Street, Silver Street, Tin Street; 'Hàng' means 'merchandise') (invert: the 36 guild-streets is the hook). T2: at the quarter's edge sits Hoan Kiem Lake, the 'Lake of the Returned Sword', named for the legend of King Le Loi, who handed a magic sword back to a giant golden turtle that rose from the water (label LEGEND). T3: Hanoi is one of Asia's oldest capitals — founded in 1010 as Thang Long, 'City of the Ascending Dragon'. T4: the city grew on the flood-prone Red River delta and is ringed by earthen dikes that hold the river back; its very name, Hà Nội, means 'inside the river's bend' (teach 'delta / dike'). Extra rungs: the tube-house shophouses, narrow at the front and long behind; the red arched Huc Bridge to the lake's island temple; the French Quarter's tree-lined boulevards beside the old town.
source: Wikipedia (Hanoi, Hoan Kiem Lake, Old Quarter of Hanoi); Facts and Details (Old Quarter of Hanoi); Ancient-Origins (Hoan Kiem legend)
framing_note: Voice: scene-led; the guild-street maze and the sword lake are the anchors. Key accuracy rail: the returned-sword story is LEGEND — attribute as 'according to legend'; the founding of Thang Long (1010) and the meaning of Hà Nội are the settled facts. Dinner-test payoff: the streets still named for their trades. Lane borders: the lake's giant softshell turtle is a real animal but keep the answer the PLACE-legend, not the turtle's biology (animal bank); Hanoi's pho and street food belong to the COOKING bank — no food-origin rung.

name: Hue Imperial Citadel
scope: The last imperial capital of Vietnam, on the Perfume River. T1: on the river's north bank stands the Imperial Citadel of Hue — a vast square fortress of moats, gates and brick ramparts that was the home of Vietnam's last emperors (the Nguyen dynasty, 1802–1945). T2: deep inside lies the Forbidden Purple City, an inner palace so private that only the emperor, his family and eunuch servants could enter — modeled on Beijing's Forbidden City. T3: the river winding past is the Perfume River (Sông Hương), named for the scent of flowers that drift into it from orchards upstream in autumn. T4: scattered in the pine hills around Hue are the grand garden-TOMBS the Nguyen emperors built for themselves — walled palaces of pavilions, lotus ponds and stelae, some designed and used as retreats while the emperor still lived. Extra rungs: the seven-tiered Thien Mu Pagoda on a bluff over the river; the Meridian Gate (Ngo Mon) entrance; the layered nesting of Capital City, Imperial City and Forbidden Purple City.
source: Wikipedia (Imperial City of Huế); UNESCO World Heritage (Complex of Huế Monuments, #678); vietnamdiscovery.com (Forbidden Purple City)
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the nested citadel and the Perfume River are the scenes. Key accuracy rail: the 'Forbidden Purple City' name deliberately echoes Beijing's — that parallel is the T2 wonder; the Perfume River's name comes from upstream flowers (fact, tell it as such). Dinner-test payoff: the emperors' garden-tombs designed to be lived in before death. Distractors stay live with other real Asian palace-cities (Beijing's Forbidden City, Seoul's Gyeongbokgung).
history_overlap: The Nguyen dynasty's political history is a history-bank topic; keep rungs anchored to the physical citadel, the river and the tombs.

name: Bali: Uluwatu & the Subak
scope: The Hindu island of Bali, its cliff-temples, rice terraces and volcanoes. T1: the sea-temple of Uluwatu clings to the edge of a sheer cliff 70 m above the crashing Indian Ocean — its name even means 'rock's end' (ulu = tip, watu = rock) (invert: the cliff-edge temple is the hook; teach the name). T2: Bali is ringed with such sea-temples, meant to be seen from the water and to guard the coast — Tanah Lot perches on its own rock, cut off by the sea twice a day at high tide. T3: Bali's emerald rice terraces are watered by the Subak — a 1,000-year-old system of shared canals, weirs and water-temples where farmers cooperatively divide every drop flowing down from the volcanoes (UNESCO 2012; teach 'Subak'). T4: all that water and rich soil come from Bali's volcanoes — sacred Mount Agung, the island's highest peak, whose ash makes the fields fertile and whose summit the Balinese hold to be the home of the gods (earth-process: volcanic soil). T5: the whole Subak landscape runs on a philosophy called Tri Hita Karana — harmony among people, nature and the divine — which is why the water-temples sit exactly at the springs and fork-points that control the flow. Extra rungs: the stepped Tegallalang rice terraces; the crater lake of Mount Batur; the kecak fire-dance performed on the Uluwatu cliff at sunset.
source: Wikipedia (Uluwatu Temple, Subak (irrigation)); UNESCO World Heritage (Cultural Landscape of Bali Province: the Subak System, #1194)
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the cliff-edge temple and the terraced landscape are the scenes. Key accuracy rail: Subak is genuinely an engineered COOPERATIVE water system (not just 'pretty rice fields') and the fertility genuinely comes from volcanic ash — those are the earth/culture wonders; describe the temples respectfully. Dinner-test payoff: Uluwatu on the 70 m cliff, or the water-temples placed exactly on the springs. Distractors stay live with other real cliff/sea temples and terraced landscapes.

name: Manila: Intramuros
scope: The old Spanish walled city inside modern Manila, in the Philippines. T1: in the middle of the sprawling modern capital stands Intramuros — Latin for 'within the walls' — a whole Spanish colonial town sealed behind massive stone ramparts and a moat, begun in 1571 (teach the name 'Intramuros'). T2: its oldest survivor is San Agustin Church, finished in 1607 — the oldest stone church in the Philippines. T3: in 1945 the Battle of Manila leveled almost everything inside the walls; of the seven great churches of Intramuros, San Agustin was the ONLY one left standing. T4: Manila grew where the Pasig River empties into Manila Bay, a huge sheltered natural harbor famous for its sunsets — the very prize the Spanish, and later others, fought so hard to hold. Extra rungs: Fort Santiago guarding the river mouth; the walls built partly from adobe and coral stone; the grid of the walled quarter with the cathedral at its heart.
source: Wikipedia (Intramuros, San Agustin Church (Manila)); UNESCO World Heritage (Baroque Churches of the Philippines, 1993); National Museum of the Philippines (San Agustin Church)
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the walled city and the lone surviving church are the anchors. Key accuracy rail: Intramuros founded 1571, San Agustin completed 1607 and the only Intramuros church to survive the 1945 battle — keep these exact. Dinner-test payoff: seven churches, one survivor (T3). Colonialism honest BOTH ways: the walls were Spain's fortress that literally kept Filipinos 'outside the walls' (extra muros), AND the Spanish left the enduring architecture and faith that define the city today — state both plainly, no cheerleading and no sneering. History overlap noted below.
history_overlap: The Spanish conquest and the 1945 Battle of Manila are history-bank episodes; here they explain the WALLS and why only one church survived — keep the rungs on the physical walled city and San Agustin, not the campaigns.

name: Hoi An
scope: The perfectly preserved old trading port on the Thu Bon River in central Vietnam. T1: Hoi An is crossed by a 400-year-old Japanese Covered Bridge — a wooden footbridge with a small temple built into its middle, its two ends guarded by carved dog and monkey statues. T2: the town froze in time because its harbor SILTED UP — the Thu Bon River filled the old port with mud, so the sea trade moved to nearby Da Nang and left the merchant town almost untouched for centuries (earth-process: siltation). T3: on every full moon the town switches off its electric lights and floats hundreds of glowing silk lanterns down the river. Optional extra: the yellow-washed merchant shophouses of the old town, a UNESCO-listed trading port that mixed Vietnamese, Chinese and Japanese quarters.
source: Wikipedia (Hội An, Japanese Covered Bridge / Chùa Cầu); UNESCO World Heritage (Hoi An Ancient Town, 1999)
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; three gem rungs, each a different concrete wonder. Key accuracy rail: the town is preserved BECAUSE the harbor silted and trade left — that siltation is the real geographic cause (the T2 dinner-test payoff), not just 'it's old'. Lane border (COOKING): Hoi An's famous cao lau noodles belong to the cooking bank — a passing mention is fine, no food-origin rung. Distractors stay live with other real preserved ports/bridges.
